Well, a person might have a 'natural weight' in the sense that their height (mostly) and body structure (I'm talking broad shoulders vs small frame, for example, not "I naturally have a lot of fat on my body") determine their healthy weight.

I think the phenomenon you're trying to describe is the result of how the body functions from an energy perspective. Everyone has a rate at which they expend energy strictly to stay alive. It's called the basal metabolic rate and it is the number of calories per day that someone's body burns in order to carry out basic, involuntary functions like digestion. It's dependent on the current state of the body, especially weight.

A person weighing 300 lbs and standing 6 feet tall might have a BMR of 2500 calories a day. So, if they eat 2500 calories a day and do not exercise at all, then the difference between consumption and expenditure is zero. When there is no net difference, a person tends to maintain their weight. But, if they either eat 500 fewer calories per day OR burn 500 extra calories through exercise, they suddenly have a deficit of 500 calories. When the body operates at a deficit, it turns to fat stores to make up the difference—so routinely burning more than you consume will always cause weight loss, barring unusual medical situations. 

The thing is, if the individual loses 50 lbs doing this, then their new weight means that their body now needs less energy to operate normally. If they needed 2500 calories at 300 lbs and changed their diet so that they were eating only 2000 for a while and lost that weight, maybe now they only need 2200 calories to function and maintain their weight. If they're still eating 2000 at this point, then the weight will be coming off more slowly because the deficit is now only 200 calories per day (as a rule of thumb, a pound of fat is equivalent to about 3500 cal).

Some people don't realize that they need to be adjusting their diet after significant weight loss. Essentially you have more leeway when you're very overweight than when you just have a few pounds to lose.

Diet sodas are really only 'terrible' from a nutritional perspective: they have pretty much no nutrients for your body. BUT, unless someone can explain to me otherwise, 'hidden calories' is a ridiculous term. The calories on the label are what the drink contains (per serving, of course). That's the energy you take in by drinking it and that's what your body has to burn to counteract it. No more, no less.

That said, you mentioned you're exercising, which is good of course, but weight loss is much, much easier to attain by focusing on diet. If you don't eat it in the first place, you don't have to burn it off. At 6'1" and 250, your body needs somewhere around 2193 calories a day. A pound of fat is ~3500 calories, so if you eat only 1693 calories a day (call it 1700) you will already lose about a pound a week. Without having to exercise at all. Any workout you do on top of that would help you lose it faster and probably build some muscle.
